summary: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis is the most common presentation, but the highest-stakes decision is recognizing acute chest syndrome early and knowing when simple transfusion isn't enough — exchange transfusion has specific indications, and pushing hemoglobin too high with simple transfusion alone can make things worse.
whyThisMatters: Sickle cell patients are frequently undertreated for pain due to stigma and bias, while the genuinely dangerous complications (acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration, priapism) can be under-recognized because a 'routine' pain crisis presentation is so much more common — both failure modes cause real, preventable harm.
clinicalTakeaway:
PAIN: treat aggressively and per the patient's individualized pain plan where one exists — they know their own disease.

Actively screen every sickle cell presentation for the complications that change management:
- new hypoxia or infiltrate = acute chest syndrome until proven otherwise
- focal neuro deficit = stroke
- priapism > 4h = urologic emergency

TRANSFUSION: reserve exchange transfusion for its specific indications (stroke, moderate-to-severe acute chest syndrome, multiorgan dysfunction) rather than reflexively transfusing everyone, and never push hemoglobin above ~10 g/dL with simple transfusion alone.

items: Believe the patient — they typically know their own crisis pattern and often have a documented individualized pain management plan; follow it when available rather than defaulting to a generic weak-opioid pathway.

Aggressive analgesia, typically IV opioids, dosed to effect and reassessed frequently — undertreatment of sickle cell pain is a well-documented, real problem driven by bias, and it delays recovery, not just comfort.

IV fluids at a maintenance (not aggressive/bolus) rate for most crises — overhydration doesn't shorten a vaso-occlusive crisis and can contribute to volume overload/precipitate acute chest syndrome in a susceptible patient.
Incentive spirometry for any hospitalized patient — reduces atelectasis, which is itself a risk factor for precipitating acute chest syndrome.
Actively look for a precipitant (infection, dehydration, cold exposure, hypoxia) and treat it in parallel.

body.text: Acute chest syndrome — the complication to actively rule out

Defined as a NEW pulmonary infiltrate on imaging PLUS at least one of: fever, chest pain, hypoxia, tachypnea, or wheeze/cough, in a patient with known sickle cell disease. It can look identical to a vaso-occlusive crisis or pneumonia at first and can develop or worsen AFTER admission for what looked like a routine pain crisis — have a low threshold to re-image and recheck oxygenation if a hospitalized sickle cell patient's respiratory status changes.

items: Supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, incentive spirometry, bronchodilators if wheezing, and empiric antibiotics (atypical coverage included, since the presentation overlaps with infectious pneumonia and the two often coexist).

Transfusion is a mainstay of treatment: simple transfusion may suffice for milder cases, but moderate-to-severe acute chest syndrome (significant hypoxia, multilobar involvement, rapid progression) generally warrants exchange transfusion rather than simple transfusion.

body.text: Exchange transfusion — specific indications, not routine

items: Acute ischemic stroke, or symptoms concerning for one, in a sickle cell patient — transfuse (exchange preferred) to bring HbS below ~30% pending further workup; this is one of the clearest, most time-sensitive indications.
Multiorgan dysfunction from sickle cell crisis.

Severe or refractory priapism not responding to initial measures (though evidence for transfusion specifically improving priapism outcomes is weaker than for the other indications — a shunt/drainage procedure is often the more directly effective intervention).
Preoperatively before surgery requiring general anesthesia, and in complicated pregnancy — per hematology involvement.

body.text: Do NOT push hemoglobin above roughly 10 g/dL with SIMPLE transfusion — sickle cell blood is already more viscous than normal, and adding volume without reducing the sickle-hemoglobin fraction can worsen viscosity-related complications rather than help. This is exactly the scenario exchange transfusion is designed to avoid: it replaces sickle cells with normal cells (lowering %HbS) while controlling the hematocrit rise, rather than just adding more (partly sickle) blood on top.
Other complications to keep on the differential

items: Splenic sequestration (more common in children, before autosplenectomy occurs): acute splenic enlargement with a rapid hemoglobin drop and potential shock — a genuine emergency.
Priapism > 4 hours is a urologic emergency requiring prompt intervention (aspiration/irrigation, phenylephrine) — don't let it sit while other issues are addressed.
Aplastic crisis (classically parvovirus B19): sudden, severe anemia from marrow suppression rather than hemolysis — reticulocyte count is low, distinguishing it from a typical hemolytic picture.

buildNote: Kept centered on the two highest-yield ED/ICU decisions — aggressive appropriate pain control, and recognizing which complications need transfusion escalation beyond simple pain management — rather than attempting a full hematology textbook treatment of sickle cell disease.
